source_title: Woman uses inheritance to protect 140-acre Canadian island forest
source_excerpt: A woman who used her grandmotherâs inheritance to buy a piece of land on Lasqueti Island 45 years ago has helped create a large, connected conservation area in Canada's Salish Sea. Domena Diesing and her partner, Bruce Fleming-Smith, worked with the BC Parks Foundation to permanently protect 140 acres of mature forest on their property. They kept their 20-acre home and surrounding land. The deal was combined with the purchase of the neighbouring 190.6-acre Jenkins Bay property, bringing the total newly protected land to more than 330 acres. By connecting these two properties with the existing Lasqueti Island Ecological Reserve and Mount Trematon Nature Reserve, conservation groups have created a continuous protected area covering more than 1,000 acres. According to an official announcement published by the BC Parks Foundation on 1 October 2026, this connected area is one of the largest protected natural landscapes in the Salish Sea region.Investing an inheritance to save a forestThe story of the land's protection began in 1981, when Diesing moved to Canada's West Coast from Germany in search of a place to settle. She was upset by the large areas of clear-cut forests she saw along the coastline. She decided to use money inherited from her grandmother to buy a share in a 160-acre property on Lasqueti Island. Having grown up around Germany's heavily managed forests, Diesing was drawn to the island's wild and untouched ancient woodland. After meeting Fleming-Smith, the couple built a home among the trees. Over several years, they gradually bought the remaining shares of the property from its other owners. For more than four decades, the couple carefully looked after the land. They tried to limit their impact on the environment and avoided activities such as burning leftover branches and wood from logging. Instead, they focused on keeping the forest and its natural ecosystem intact.Protecting rare coastal ecosystemsAs the years passed, Diesing and Fleming-Smith began looking for legal ways to make sure the land would remain protected after their deaths. The couple joined hands with the BC Parks Foundation and donated part of their property's value through Canada's Ecological Gift program. Under the agreement, 140 acres were placed under permanent public protection, while the couple kept their original 20-acre home property. âWe were able to actually make a gesture that would pass on the responsibilities of stewardship that we had felt with our ownership over the years, pass that on to the public and to future generations,â Fleming-Smith said in statements documented by the BC Parks Foundation. The protected land, known as the Jenkins Creek property, is part of the Coastal Douglas-fir maritime ecosystem. This is one of the rarest and most threatened natural areas in British Columbia. According to survey information provided by the BC Parks Foundation, the property contains several rare plant communities. These include Douglas-fir and Arbutus, Douglas-fir and Dull Oregon-grape, as well as Grand fir and Three-leaved foamflower. The area also has several seasonal streams that flow into Jenkins Creek. This creek is an important waterway for salmon and runs through the valley before reaching Jenkins Cove.Honouring a neighbor's fifteen year visionThe protection of Jenkins Creek happened alongside the long-awaited conservation of the neighbouring 190.6-acre Jenkins Bay property. This completed a conservation effort that had been in the works for more than 15 years. The Jenkins Bay property belonged to the late Alfred âAlâ Gaensbauer. He was a local warden for the nearby Lasqueti Island Ecological Reserve and spent decades caring for the area's natural environment. Around 2011, Gaensbauer began working with conservationists Sheila Harrington and Gordon Scott, president of the Lasqueti Island Nature Conservancy, to find a permanent way to protect his property. Gaensbauer also took part in local environmental projects. He helped restore local fish populations and carried out the first official nest counts of Pigeon Guillemots living on nearby coastal cliffs. Research carried out on his property by ecologist Terry McIntosh also found rare lichens and mosses, including the Rigid Apple Moss, which is listed as threatened at the federal level. After Gaensbauer died, his family continued working with the BC Parks Foundation and local organisers to carry out his original plans for the land. âAl was very fit and spry well into his late eighties,â Scott recalled in statements published by the BC Parks Foundation. âHe built his own home, lifting timbers with ropes and pulleys, and developed an orchard and garden, disturbing as little of the surrounding forest as possible.â Harrington said completing the transfer fulfilled a long-standing promise to Gaensbauer and the local community. It also ensures that the combined 330-acre area will remain protected from development and disturbance indefinitely.A growing network of island reservesThe conservation efforts aimed at protecting Jenkins Creek and Jenkins Bay contribute to a series of other significant environmental initiatives undertaken by various conservation organizations on Lasqueti Island in the previous years. In the year 2025, the BC Parks Foundation successfully collaborated with local property owners to secure the preservation of two distinct parcels of land located in the southwestern region of the island. When combined with the foundation's acquisition of Point Young in 2022, these transactions culminated in the establishment of a protected zone that encompasses an impressive total of 568 acres surrounding Squitty Bay Park. Andy Day, who serves as the chief executive officer of the BC Parks Foundation, remarked that the establishment of this newly connected reserveâspanning over 1,000 acresâdemonstrates the remarkable outcomes achievable through sustained cooperation among local residents. "This remarkable achievement is yet another illustration of what can be accomplished when individuals demonstrate a deep care for the land, join forces, and adopt a long-term perspective," Day expressed in the official release from the foundation. "Al dedicated several decades to the stewardship of this land and was eager to see it preserved. Domena and Bruce made a substantial financial contribution. The commitment of local conservationists has persisted for more than ten years, and once again, our donor community has risen to the occasion." With the legal protection now firmly established, this unified area is set to play a crucial role in safeguarding vital coastal shorelines, ancient forests, and fish habitats throughout the Salish Sea for the benefit of future generations. The newly protected landscape will also strengthen the islandâs wider conservation network, helping preserve its ecological diversity and natural heritage for generations to come.
